slides.0.title: Grape varieties
slides.0.subtitle: Malbec, Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Torrontés, Chardonnay and the Criolla family
slides.1.title: Malbec: the flagship
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Area
slides.1.highlights.0.content: 46,941 ha (Wines of Argentina, cited by Forbes Argentina on 15 May 2024), about a quarter of vineyard area and over 40% of red grape area; up 195% since 2010
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Distribution
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Mendoza has 84.4%, followed by San Juan and Salta
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Exports
slides.1.highlights.2.content: In 2023 Malbec made up 69.3% of the volume of exported varietal wine (INV)
slides.1.content: Malbec is both Argentina's largest red grape and the mainstay of its exports.
slides.2.title: Other red grapes
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Bonarda
slides.2.highlights.0.content: 17,448 ha in 2022, 8.4% of national vineyard area and the second most planted red after Malbec (INV); 84.1% is in Mendoza and 11.5% in San Juan
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Tempranillo
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Syrah grew from 700 ha in 1990 to over 10,000 ha (Wikipedia, figures around 2003)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The Criolla family
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Criolla Grande, Cereza and Criolla Chica historically made up about 25–30% of plantings (Wikipedia and Wine With Seth differ) and mostly go into bulk wine
slides.2.content: After Malbec, Bonarda is the second red; the Criolla family were historically the raw material of bulk wine.
slides.3.title: Whites: Torrontés and others
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Torrontés Riojano
slides.3.highlights.0.content: A natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica (2003 DNA study); 7,075 ha in 2024, about 80% of Torrontés area; best at altitude, around 1,700 m in Cafayate
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Three Torrontés
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Riojano, Sanjuanino and Mendocino; Riojano is the most planted and best regarded
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Pedro Giménez, Chardonnay and others
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Pedro Giménez was the most planted white (Wikipedia, figures around 2003), followed by Muscat of Alexandria and Chardonnay
slides.3.content: Torrontés is Argentina's most distinctive white: dry, intensely aromatic, with a Muscat character.
slides.4.title: Diploma depth: why Malbec succeeded in Argentina, and Bonarda’s true identity
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Malbec’s weaknesses in France
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Malbec (Côt in Cahors) is frost-sensitive and prone to coulure (poor fruit set), and in humid Bordeaux it is disease-prone; the severe frost of February 1956 devastated Bordeaux Malbec and many growers replanted other varieties, while Cahors replanted Malbec
slides.4.highlights.1.title: What Argentina solved
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Dry, low rainfall and strong sun → low disease pressure and healthy fruit; the diurnal range and strong UV at altitude → thick skins, deep colour, supple tannins and retained acidity. Most of Malbec’s French weaknesses are not issues here, which is why it became Argentina’s signature
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Bonarda is really Douce Noir
slides.4.highlights.2.content: DNA studies show Argentina’s “Bonarda” is unrelated to Italian Bonarda; it is Douce Noir from Savoie in France (also called Corbeau, and Charbono in California); researchers proposed the name “Bonarda from Argentina” to distinguish it
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Bonarda’s role
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Bonarda is high-yielding and late-ripening, mostly in the warmer eastern lowlands of Mendoza, and was long used for bulk and blending; some producers now make juicy, soft-tannined varietal wines from low-yielding old vines as a second calling card after Malbec
slides.4.content: The formula for a variety’s success: its weaknesses at home + how the new region solves them.
